person: Rosa Villanueva is a 64-year-old retired school cafeteria manager in Texas who keeps her family's papers in folders by property. She has a recall letter for her 2022 Kestrel's fuel pump and a folder of repair invoices from the shop, plus a separate one for her husband Hector's older truck, which is not in the recall. She wants to be reimbursed only for what she truly paid for the recall repair, and she dislikes legal words and small text. Hector says to forget it, but she does not like leaving money on the table.
stated_up_front: I got a recall letter about the fuel pump on my Kestrel and I have the repair papers right here in the folder. Can you figure out which of the charges I can get my money back for? Please don't put in anything that isn't right.

facts.truth: Her 2022 Kestrel is in the fuel pump recall; the letter came in August 2026.

facts.about: Fuel pump module repair at the shop
facts.truth: Replaced in November 2025; she paid $212.00 labour and a $18.50 shop fee herself.
She bought the module herself for $289.00 plus $17.34 sales tax, and has the receipt in the folder.
A fuel pump relay was fixed in May 2025 for $96.00, before the plan's window opened.
They were on the same November invoice, $74.90 together, and are not part of the recall.
A second pump was replaced in March 2026 under the parts warranty and she paid $0.
She was towed once in February 2026 and her roadside cover paid the $135 bill.
A $40 core deposit was charged on the part and refunded to her afterward.
Hector's older Kestrel had a fuel pump job for $310 in 2025, but its VIN is not in the recall.
Car papers are in a blue folder marked 'Kestrel' in the drawer by the desk, separate from the property folders.

unknowns: Whether the plan's start and end dates are the ones that apply to her claim
Whether the shop fee counts as part of the recall repair
Why the relay repair was not covered by the recall
What the federal rule number on the carmaker's letter means for her
